draft.title: Writing accents and dialects
card: An accent is how words sound when someone speaks. A writer can show it by changing spelling, such as writing "gonna" or "ya" for the way a character says the words.
A dialect is a way of speaking shared by a group or region. It has its own words and grammar, such as "we was" or "youse" for "you" when speaking to more than one person.
Writers use these changes to show where a character is from, or what their background and personality are like. A few well-chosen changes are enough for a reader to hear the voice.
Take care. If every word is altered, the text is hard to read. If only some characters are written this way, it can make them look silly or less clever, which is mockery.
draft.remember: Change a few words to give a character a voice, and do it with respect.

a.q: A writer has a character say "We was late 'cause the bus never come." What is the writer showing through this grammar?
opts: The character's dialect
The character's loud volume
The character's lie
The character's age only
a.why: Forms like "we was" and "never come" are grammar used by a group of speakers, so they show a dialect. Volume is not shown by grammar, and nothing here suggests a lie.
a.clue: Think about grammar shared by a group of speakers.

b.q: In a story, only the farm worker Jed has his speech written with heavy spelling changes. The others speak in standard English. What is the main risk?
opts: Jed may look silly or less clever to readers
Jed's lines will be too short to follow
Jed's lines will sound like the narrator
The other characters will sound more rural
b.why: Changing only one character's speech heavily can make readers laugh at him or see him as less clever, which is mockery. The spelling changes do not shorten his lines, and they set him apart from the narrator rather than making him sound like it.
b.clue: Ask what readers may think when only one person is written this way.

b.best: Jed may look silly or less clever to readers
